h: A concrete village with a poet in its heart
p: The Barbican Estate rose from an area of the City badly damaged by bombing in the Second World War. Built between the 1960s and 1970s, with the arts centre opening in 1982, it was designed as a self-contained village of homes, schools, gardens, lakes and culture, linked by raised walkways above the traffic. Today it's Grade II listed, and whether you think it's a brutalist masterpiece or a concrete maze, it's undeniably one of a kind.

Wander a little and history pokes through the modern blocks. Fragments of the old Roman and medieval London Wall can be seen around the edges of the estate, and right in the middle of it all sits St Giles Cripplegate, a medieval church that survived the Blitz in part. John Milton, author of Paradise Lost, is buried there, which is a lovely surprise to stumble on among the concrete towers.

Inside the centre, the Barbican Art Gallery hosts big exhibitions, while The Curve, a long, sweeping gallery space, often has free shows and installations. The Barbican Cinema screens everything from new releases to classic seasons, and the Barbican Hall's programme ranges from orchestral concerts to gigs and world music.

Allow plenty of time if you're new to the place, as finding your way around is part of the adventure. Grab a map at the entrance and follow the yellow lines on the walkways. Once you've had your fill, Postman's Park, a small garden with a touching memorial to everyday heroes, is a short walk south, and the Farringdon end of town is great for a post-show bite. Smithfield's grand Victorian meat market buildings are close by too, and they make a striking sight even if you're only passing through on your way to dinner.
